newsitem.title: MEXICO: Peasants bussed in, given flags to greet Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Peasants bussed in, given flags to greet Clinton.

text.p: Crowds of pro-government Mexicans were given U.S. flags, packed lunches and a free ride to this quiet southern town on Wednesday to greet President Bill Clinton, whose trip to Mexico was being carefully managed to avoid any embarrassing protests.

For Clinton's first encounter with "ordinary" Mexicans, kept until the last day of his three-day visit, the colonial city of Tlaxcala 75 miles (120 km) east of Mexico City could not have been better chosen as the epitome of sunny, laid-back, trouble-free Mexico.

Long in the grip of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), picturesque Tlaxcala suffers none of the grinding poverty, political violence or guerrilla revolts that afflict other Mexican tourist destinations such as Oaxaca or Chiapas.
Thousands of peasants, wearing donated Tlaxcala baseball caps, and waving Mexican and U.S. flags, were bussed in by the government on Wednesday to see their first visiting foreign president.

They expressed fierce loyalty to President Ernesto Zedillo and warm support for his guests, Clinton and wife Hillary, even though there was muffled anger over U.S. immigration laws that threaten many Mexicans with deportation.

"If we went there, they would send us back here with a boot up the backside, but our arms are wide open to Clinton," said a smiling Alberta Fernandez Martinez, a peasant from the town of Huamantla in the state of Tlaxcala.

Surrounded by hundreds of fellow farm workers, she said that all the local supporters of Zedillo's PRI had been invited to see Clinton, much in the way that they are bussed to political rallies to support the party, which has ruled Mexico for 68 unbroken years.
Besides the chance of a day out, they were given the usual prize for attendance -- a sandwich, two oranges and a fruit juice.
"This is Clinton: we ought to be eating McDonalds, not bread like ducks", a friend of Fernandez Martinez joked."
There was no opposition support or anti-American sentiment visible within blocks of the spruced up city square where Clinton was expected to press the flesh later.

"Tlaxcala is one of the most peaceful cities in Mexico. That is why they are bringing Clinton here," said Jose Luis Guetierrez, keyboard player in a pop band that was warming up to keep the waiting crowds entertained.

Not taking any chances even with the carefully selected crowd, heavily armed troops, explosives experts and sharpshooters even in the belltower of Tlaxcala's main church, were at the ready since dawn.
Crowds lining up to enter the square were searched with metal detectors, suspicious-looking bags of foods were confiscated and street vendors were turned away.

But locals who faced any inconvenience largely shrugged it off, noting that Tlaxcala -- one of the first Mexican towns to welcome Spanish conquistadors as allies against their Aztec enemies in the 16th century -- was well-known for its warmth to foreigners.
"They call us traitors in the rest of Mexico," said shoeshiner Silvino Varela Sanchez. "But we have a saying here: 'If you can't beat your enemy, join him.'"
